newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac backs Britain over working week.
newsitem.headline: Chirac backs Britain over working week.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac offered surprise support to Britain on Friday in its showdown with the European Union over whether it can impose a maximum working week in Britain.

At the end of a two-day Franco-British summit, British Prime Minister John Major renewed threats to seek changes to EU law if the European Court of Justice rules to ban workers in many British industries from working more than 48 hours a week.
Major portrayed the conflict as a matter of principle to stem fears that the EU was dictating too many aspects of European life.
Before Major spoke, Chirac was asked if he backed Major.

"Regarding the conflict between the Court of Justice and Britain...I am very close to John Major in this matter and completely prepared to give him my backing," he told a news conference in Bordeaux, south-west France.
A British government spokesman said of Chirac's remarks: "We have made our reasoned arguments quite clear. We welcome his support."
Some French officials, however, suggested that Chirac may not have intended such unequivocal endorsement and had meant to talk in general terms about Britain's ability to contest court rulings.

The court will rule on Tuesday on Britain's challenge to the 1993 directive 93/104/EC fixing maximum working hours. If past cases are a guide, the court is likely to endorse the opinion of an advocate-general that went against Britain.
"If we lose, we will need to seek a change to the (Maastricht) treaty," he told the news conference after a two-day summit.
The issue would have to be taken up by the inter-governmental conference (IGC) struggling through a review of EU institutions ahead of planned enlargement of the Union.
Major said a ruling against Britain would violate the spirit of an opt-out Britain obtained in 1991 from the Social Chapter on workplace standards under Maastricht.
Major also said working hours were mainly an issue for employees and employers and that it was not the EU's job to impose "prescriptive judgments" on individual nations.
He said it was an issue of principle, saying that the sme treaty provisions treaty could "be used to drive through other legislation."
